title: Playing traditional bands and singing Mardi Gras Indian words
summary: Most work now comes from traditional bands; he surprised the interviewer by singing Creole and Indian chant words.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Yeah. So now you play a lot of jobs with traditional jazz bands all around the Bay Area. I mean, you're playing.
Yes.
Yeah.
Most of my work is coming from them now.
What was surprising to me, I remember one night we played, you were playing with the band, and we played that tune called Do What Or He Says.
Yeah.
And then out of the blue, you just started singing these old Creole lyrics.
Yeah.
I mean, you hadn't sung that for how long? I mean, you probably hadn't...
Oh, been about 50, maybe about 55 years.
But those words had to come out of your mouth. Did you know a lot of those? I like the Creole tunes. I mean, you know...
No, well, the words I put there was from the old Indian song, the old Mardi Gras Indian song. Yeah. Pacafinoja.
Yeah. Paco...
Pacafinoja.
Yeah.
And they had Pacafinoja. It's just according to who was saying those things. So I just used that as the old Indian Mardi Gras, what we call Mardi Gras language.
Yeah. So the lyrics, Do What Or He Says became transformed to Pacafinoja.
Yeah. Yeah.
I thought that was pretty interesting.
Oh, I agree.
